title: Which graph algorithm do I need?
sub: Answer a few questions about your problem.

start.q: What do you need to find?

sp_scope.q: From one source, or between every pair?

sp_weights.q: What are the edge weights like?

sp_target.q: Do you only care about one specific target, and have a good estimate of distance to it?

options.label: Yes, one target with a good estimate

sp_dag.q: Is the graph a DAG (directed, with no cycles)?

mst_dense.q: Is the graph sparse or dense?

options.label: Directed: who can reach whom both ways

comp_dyn.q: Is the graph fixed, or do edges keep arriving?

bfs.why: In an unweighted graph the first time BFS reaches a vertex is along a path with the fewest edges. O(V + E).

dijkstra.why: With no negative weights, the closest unfinished vertex is safe to finalize. O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

astar.why: Dijkstra guided by an estimate of the remaining distance. If the estimate never overestimates, it's still optimal, and explores far less.

bf.why: Relaxes every edge V − 1 times instead of finalizing greedily, so negative weights are fine, and one extra round detects negative cycles. O(VE).

dagdp.why: With no cycles, process vertices in topological order and each one is final when you reach it. Negative weights are fine, longest paths too. O(V + E).

fw.why: Adds one allowed stopover vertex at a time. Handles negative edges (not negative cycles). O(V³), so best up to a few hundred vertices; for large sparse graphs, run Dijkstra from every source instead.

kruskal.why: Sort the edges and add each unless it closes a cycle, checked with Union-Find. O(E log E).

prim.why: Grow one tree, always adding the cheapest edge out of it. With a simple array it's O(V²), ideal for dense graphs.

arbo.why: Kruskal and Prim assume edges work both ways. The directed version, a minimum spanning arborescence from a root, needs Edmonds' algorithm.

topo.why: Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly output something with no unmet prerequisites) or reversed DFS finish order. If it can't finish, there's a circular dependency. O(V + E).

bfsdfs.why: Each fresh search from an unvisited vertex finds one connected component. O(V + E).

uf.why: Merges components as edges arrive and answers 'same component?' in near-constant amortized time.

scc.why: Two DFS passes, the second on the reversed graph, find every strongly connected component. O(V + E).

flow.answer: Max flow (Edmonds-Karp, or Dinic for speed)
flow.why: Augment along paths with spare capacity until none remain. Bipartite matching is max flow with all capacities 1.

dfs_dir.why: Running into a vertex that's still on the current DFS path means a cycle. O(V + E).

uf_cycle.why: In an undirected graph, an edge to an already-visited vertex other than your parent closes a cycle; Union-Find spots an edge joining two vertices already connected.
